A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The WildBench material in v1 Appendix C matches v3 Appendix E; the additional appendices can be distinguished from relocated content.

before.justification: v1 reports original disagreement analyses, reward-model experiments, and LLM-as-Judge evaluations, including quantitative results in Tables 1–5 and WildBench case studies.

after.justification: v3 retains those original empirical results and adds evaluations of Skywork and Nemotron reward models and additional reward-distribution analyses.

M1.justification: The Mean-Variance KL model, tie-based correlation, preference intervals, classification reward model, and WildBench filtering procedure are retained. Section 4 clarifies that the classification divisiveness score multiplies the probabilities of labels 1 and 5; this documents the existing score rather than establishing a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions use MultiPref, HelpSteer2, the Anthropic Harmless subset, CocoNot underspecified prompts, and WildBench for the same tasks. The added large-model evaluations reuse MultiPref. Appendix C newly describes existing annotator populations rather than introducing different populations.

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 add Skywork-Reward-Gemma-2-27B-v0.2 and Llama-3.1-Nemotron-70B-Reward while retaining the earlier comparators. These external large-scale models substantially broaden the comparison beyond the paper's Llama-3-8B-based systems.

E3.justification: The added 27B and 70B checkpoint evaluations are restricted to MultiPref to avoid overlap with their HelpSteer2 training data. Figure 1 now pools response permutations as well as annotator permutations. The existing training budgets, evaluation metrics, and stated held-out evaluation setup are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix D and Figures 4–5 extend the agreement-stratified reward-gap analysis to additional Bradley-Terry and MSE configurations and the two external models. These distributions deepen an existing diagnostic analysis. The original MultiPref Bradley-Terry histogram is also redisplayed, and the WildBench case studies remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The annotator-agreement statistics are unchanged; predicted reward variances are model outputs rather than newly added uncertainty estimates for experimental results.

E6.justification: Table 3 adds MultiPref accuracy/AUROC results of 0.651/0.494 for Skywork and 0.638/0.400 for Nemotron. Table 2 revises all four HelpSteer2 MSE(Agg) gaps, including 0.811 to 1.57 for high-agreement preferences and 0.706 to 1.22 for diverging preferences, and removes the All Examples row. Section 3 changes the substantial-divergence frequency from 0.11% to 11%. Additional distributions appear in Appendix D, while earlier Table 3 scores and judge findings are retained. The unexplained MSE revisions do not establish a performance improvement.

T1.justification: The Gaussian reward assumption, correlated reward-difference expression in Equation 1, preference-label intervals, losses, and mean-variance disagreement score are retained. No theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is added or removed.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the disagreement taxonomy, diagnosis of standard reward models and LLM judges, distributional reward modeling, and identification of divisive benchmark prompts. The new contribution bullets restate these claims, and the introduction retains the claimed 0.16 AUROC improvement.

C2.justification: Section 3 drops the stronger interpretation that substantial disagreements exaggerate reward-model decisiveness. Section 5.3 removes the option of separately evaluating divisive examples and replaces future work on pluralistic, non-binary judges with training LLMs using distributional rewards. The main interpretation of disagreement and evaluation bias remains.

D1.justification: New Appendix C documents annotator eligibility, recruitment platforms, and counts: 189 Prolific annotators for MultiPref and roughly 1,000 Scale AI workers for HelpSteer2. Section 4 clarifies the classification score computation. Existing hyperparameters and hardware details remain, but Table 2 loses subset counts and the direct HelpSteer2 disagreements-data link is removed.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds work on ambiguity and veridicality and connects perspectivist annotation to social choice and value-sensitive design. Skywork and Gemma references accompany the new comparisons. The Sandri toxicity-taxonomy discussion is removed and the Pitis discussion shortened, while the overall research positioning remains similar.

P1.justification: v3 edits the abstract and prose, adds an explicit contribution list and Section 3.1 heading, shortens some discussions, and adds impact and acknowledgement sections. Appendix organization expands, but the seven-section narrative and most explanations remain recognizable rather than being substantially restructured.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a predominantly single-column layout to the ICML two-column format. Figure 1 replaces full heatmaps and marginal histograms with compact triangular displays; Tables 2–3 are restructured; Figures 4–5 add extensive histogram panels. Prompt and case-study tables are resized and relocated, producing a substantial visual revision.

improvement.justification: The added 27B and 70B comparisons strengthen the central diagnosis beyond the authors' 8B training setup, while fuller distribution plots and annotator documentation improve scrutiny of the evidence. These are useful but limited gains: the main method results remain unchanged, and unexplained MSE revisions plus removed subset counts weaken transparency in Table 2.
